text: Chapter 4 covers the tool for pixel-perfect, often scheduled output: BI Publisher, also called Oracle Analytics Publisher. Let's lay out its architecture.

Pixel-perfect means reproducing an exact layout every single time, same fonts, same column widths, same placement of a required field, no matter how much data flows through. A 1099 tax form has to match a government-specified layout exactly. A quick ad hoc list for an internal meeting doesn't need that at all, which is why OTBI handles that case instead.

Every BI Publisher report keeps two concerns separate. The data model defines where the data comes from, typically a query producing an XML structure. The template defines how that data looks, fonts, tables, headers, logos, usually built as an RTF file in Microsoft Word with the Template Builder add-in. Separating them means one data model can feed multiple templates.

A report definition ties a data model to a default template, plus any parameters that prompt the user before running, similar in spirit to a Financial Reporting Studio point of view. Running it executes the query, merges the XML with the template, and produces PDF, Excel, Word, or other output.
These three tools cooperate more than they compete. A BI Publisher data model can even pull from an existing OTBI subject area when that's convenient. Up next, lesson sixteen: building a data model.
